parts.name: Mk1 Capsule
parts.desc: One seat, basic life support. Cramped but light.
parts.role: The cabin: one seat, the controls, and the air the crew breathes.
parts.detail: The smallest cabin that keeps a person alive: a seat, a window, life support for the trip and the computer that flies the ship. Shaped like Mercury: a steep cone of dark heat-resistant shingles and a narrow neck that holds the parachutes. Light and cheap, but nothing spare: every extra bottle of oxygen is a separate part outside.
cons: One cramped seat, no spare air
parts.real: Mercury-class: the Mercury capsule was 1.89 m across the heat shield and about 1.3 t in orbit

parts.name: Mk2 Capsule
parts.desc: Roomier cabin, better instruments.
parts.role: The cabin: the crew, the controls and life support, with room to move.
parts.detail: A roomier cabin with better instruments and a little more power. A gentle cone like Gemini and Crew Dragon, with a docking ring on the nose. Still the heaviest single piece of hardware on most ships, which is why it sits on top: the rest of the stack is built to carry it.
parts.real: Gemini (2.3 m) and Crew Dragon (about 4 m)-class cabin: a 20° cone above the heat shield

parts.name: Mk3 Capsule
parts.desc: Big cabin with its own spare oxygen. Heavy.
parts.role: A big cabin with its own spare oxygen. Heavy.
parts.detail: The flagship cabin: more room, more power, a spare oxygen supply built in, and the most reliable systems. A wide blunt cone like Apollo and Orion, so the heat shield is big and the entry is gentle. The price is mass, and mass is paid in propellant.
parts.real: Apollo command module (3.9 m wide, 5.56 t, silver Mylar skin over the ablator) / Orion (5.0 m)

parts.name: Pointed nose, small
parts.desc: A slim ogive for a small stack.
parts.role: A slim nose for a small ship.
parts.detail: A small ogive fairing. Less frontal area means less drag in the thick air of the first two minutes, where most of the aerodynamic loss happens.
cons: Small: looks odd on a wide body
parts.real: Rocket Lab Electron fairing: 1.2 m × 2.5 m, 44 kg, composite clamshell, pneumatic unlock and springs

parts.name: Pointed nose cone
parts.desc: Low drag through thick air.
parts.role: A sharp nose that cuts through thick air.
parts.detail: A tangent ogive: a cylinder that curves smoothly into a point, with a boat-tail at the base that narrows down to the capsule's nose. A pointed nose has the least drag in the thick air of the first minutes of flight, which saves propellant and keeps the aerodynamic load low.
parts.real: Delta II-class fairing: the 10-ft (3.0 m) composite version is 8.9 m long with a slender nose and a rounded tip; the 9.5-ft version that carried Dawn was aluminium

parts.name: Pointed nose, large
parts.desc: A big ogive for a wide stack.
parts.role: A big nose for a wide ship.
parts.detail: A large ogive fairing for the widest bodies. More frontal area than the medium one, but the shape still cuts the air cleanly.
pros: Clean shape for a wide body
parts.real: Beyond Gravity (RUAG) 5.4 m carbon fairing: Ariane 5 (17 m, 2,675 kg), Ariane 6 (14 or 20 m), Vulcan (15.5 or 21.3 m); pyrotechnic or frangible separation

parts.name: Blunt nose cone
parts.desc: Cheaper and tougher, more drag.
parts.role: A rounded nose: cheaper, tougher, more drag.
parts.detail: A blunt nose is easier to build and takes a hit better, but pushes more air out of the way. The drag costs a little propellant on the way up.
parts.real: The payload shroud that Progress rides under on the Soyuz-2 rocket from Baikonur

parts.name: Hammerhead fairing
parts.desc: Wider than the body: room for a bulky payload.
parts.role: A fairing wider than the rocket under it.
parts.detail: A hammerhead fairing is wider than the stage below, so a bulky payload fits inside. Its own skin shields what is under it from one debris strike. The price: more drag, and a wide nose pulls the centre of pressure forward, so put bigger fins low.
pros: Shields the top from one hit
cons: Pulls the centre of pressure forward
parts.real: Atlas V 5-m fairing: 5.4 m wide, short version 20.7 m and 3,524 kg; graphite-epoxy on aluminium honeycomb (RUAG); ogive and spherical cap; it encloses the Centaur too

parts.name: Payload attach fitting
parts.desc: The cone that bolts the payload to the stage.
parts.role: The standard interface between the payload and the stage under it.
parts.detail: A truncated cone with a bolted ring at the top and a clamp band at the bottom. It carries the whole payload through launch loads, then lets it go cleanly with push-off springs. Every launcher has a standard one, so a payload built for one rocket fits another.
cons: Mass that does no work after separation
parts.real: Delta II 6915 payload attach fitting

parts.name: Spin table & clamp band
parts.desc: Spins the stage above like a rifle bullet before it fires.
parts.role: A turntable that spins the kick motor and payload for stability, and the band that releases them.
parts.detail: Small solid motors have no steering. The spin table turns the motor and payload to about 50 rpm before they separate, so gyroscopic stiffness keeps them pointed during the burn, like a thrown football. A Marman clamp band holds everything until pyrotechnic bolts cut it. Dawn was spun this way before its Star 48 fired.
parts.real: Delta II spin table and 3712 clamp band

parts.name: Kick motor, small
parts.desc: A Star-48 class third-stage motor in the stack.
parts.role: A compact solid motor that adds a final push.
parts.detail: The third-stage motor of the Dawn launch: a titanium sphere of solid propellant with a short nozzle, 66 kN for 87 seconds. Spin-stabilised, it needs no guidance of its own. Here it adds its propellant and thrust to the stack.
pros: Two tonnes of propellant in a small package
cons: Isp 286 s: worse than any liquid engine
parts.real: Star 48B: 66 kN, 286 s, 2,011 kg propellant, 126 kg empty

parts.name: Kick motor, medium
parts.desc: A larger spherical solid motor for the stack.
parts.role: A bigger kick motor: 3.3 t of solid propellant.
parts.detail: The larger spherical motor. Solid motors have the best propellant mass fraction of anything in the hangar (the case is 6 % of the mass), but the exhaust is slow: Isp 290 s.
pros: Best mass fraction in the hangar
parts.real: Star 63F / Castor 30 class

parts.name: Ablative heat shield
parts.desc: Chars away to carry the heat off. Heavy and dependable.
parts.role: An ablative shield that chars away to carry heat off.
parts.detail: The ablative heat shield burns slowly and deliberately during entry, carrying the heat away with the charred material. Heavy, dependable, and the only thing between the crew and plasma.
parts.real: Apollo Avcoat; PICA-X (Dragon 1) and PICA-3 (Crew Dragon)

parts.name: Ablative heat shield, large
parts.desc: A wider shield: more drag in thin Martian air.
parts.role: A wide ablative shield: slows the ship harder in thin air.
parts.detail: Mars has so little air that a wider shield matters: more area means more drag and a gentler, cooler entry. This one fits a large stack.
parts.real: Mars Science Laboratory 4.5 m aeroshell

parts.name: Ceramic tiles
parts.desc: Half the mass. Chips if anything hits it on the way up.
parts.role: Ceramic tiles: half the mass, chips if struck.
parts.detail: Ceramic tiles insulate instead of burning away, so they weigh half as much. They are brittle: a piece of ice or foam on ascent can crack them. Columbia was lost in 2003 when launch foam punched a hole in the carbon panels on the leading edge of its wing, and hot gas got in on entry.
cons: Chips if struck on ascent (foam chipped Shuttle tiles on many flights)
parts.real: Shuttle HRSI silica tiles

parts.name: Inflatable heat shield
parts.desc: A stack of inflatable rings under a woven ceramic cloth. Huge area, new technology.
parts.role: An inflatable aeroshell: the widest shield for the least mass.
parts.detail: Packed small for launch, inflated to a wide cone before entry: stacked rings of woven fabric under a blanket of silicon-carbide cloth. The biggest drag area of any shield, which is exactly what thin Martian air needs. It has flown once, from orbit, in 2022, so reliability is lower.
parts.real: NASA LOFTID / HIAD (2022)

parts.name: Supersonic parachute
parts.desc: Opens at Mach 1.7 in the thin Martian air.
parts.role: A supersonic parachute for the thin Martian air.
parts.detail: Mars has so little air that the chute opens at Mach 1.7 and still cannot slow the ship enough by itself. It buys time and speed before the engines light for the last kilometres.
parts.real: Perseverance 21.5 m disk-gap-band chute, opened at Mach 1.7 (Viking to Perseverance)

parts.name: Drogue chute
parts.desc: A small, strong chute that opens first and steadies the ship.
parts.role: A small chute that opens early, stops the tumbling and slows the ship a little.
parts.detail: A drogue is small and tough: it can open faster and higher than a main chute, stop the capsule tumbling, and pull the main chute out. Alone it slows the ship only a little; with a main chute it makes the whole descent gentler.
parts.real: Orion / Apollo drogue chutes

parts.name: Splash floats
parts.desc: Keeps the capsule upright after the splashdown home.
parts.role: Keeps the capsule upright after splashdown.
parts.detail: Inflatable floats for the return to Earth: they keep the capsule the right way up in the sea until the ship arrives.
pros: Keeps the capsule upright at sea
cons: Only matters on the way home
parts.real: Apollo uprighting bags

parts.name: Low-gain antenna
parts.desc: Slow but it works from anywhere.
parts.role: Slow but works from anywhere.
parts.detail: A low-gain antenna: no pointing needed, a trickle of data in any direction. Enough for voice, telemetry and small files. Without any antenna nothing you find can be sent home.
parts.real: Omnidirectional S-band LGA

parts.name: Medium-gain horn
parts.desc: A horn: faster than the omni, forgiving of pointing errors.
parts.role: A horn antenna: a useful middle between the omni and the dish.
parts.detail: A horn concentrates the signal into a wide cone. It needs only rough pointing, so it keeps working while the ship manoeuvres, and it sends data many times faster than the low-gain stick.
parts.real: Mars Odyssey medium-gain antenna

parts.name: High-gain dish
parts.desc: Uploads science fast. Must be pointed.
parts.role: Uploads science fast. Must be pointed.
parts.detail: A high-gain dish sends data hundreds of times faster, but only when it points at Earth. The science of the mission goes home through this.
parts.real: Voyager 3.7 m HGA (scaled)

parts.name: Relay smallsat
parts.desc: A small satellite left in Mars orbit to relay data home.
parts.role: A relay satellite released into Mars orbit: a dish in the sky even when Earth is below the horizon.
parts.detail: Every Mars rover talks to Earth through orbiters overhead. This smallsat rides on the side of the ship, is released into orbit, and relays data from the surface with its own dish and solar panels, so the crew can send science home even when Earth has set.
pros: Fast uploads from the surface, any time of day
parts.real: MarCO cubesats, LADEE-class bus

parts.name: RCS thruster pack
parts.desc: Small thrusters to turn the ship in space.
parts.role: Small thrusters that turn the ship in space.
parts.detail: A reaction control pack: a cluster of tiny thrusters that fire sideways to roll, pitch and yaw the ship where there is no air for fins to bite. Needed to point the ship for burns and entry.
parts.real: Shuttle forward RCS pod

parts.name: Star tracker
parts.desc: A camera that reads the stars to know which way the ship points.
parts.role: A camera that finds the ship's attitude from the star field.
parts.detail: Gyroscopes drift. A star tracker photographs the sky, matches the pattern against a catalogue of thousands of stars, and tells the computer exactly which way the ship points, to a few arcseconds. Without one the dish and the burns are pointed by dead reckoning. Reliability +0.5 %.
pros: Exact pointing for burns and the dish
parts.real: Ball CT-2020 star tracker

parts.name: Reaction wheel
parts.desc: Spins a flywheel to turn without fuel. Slow.
parts.role: Spins a flywheel to turn without fuel. Slow.
parts.detail: A spinning wheel inside the ship: speed it up and the ship turns the other way, no propellant needed. Slow and gentle; good for pointing an antenna, not for a landing.
parts.real: Dawn / Kepler reaction wheels

parts.name: Spare O₂ tank
parts.desc: A 50-litre steel bottle at 150 bar: about 10 kg of oxygen, 6 kg of it usable for the suit.
parts.role: One spare EVA oxygen refill.
parts.detail: A 50-litre steel bottle at 150 bar: about 10 kg of oxygen, 6 kg of it usable for the suit. Each trip outside costs about 2 kg: the suit's fill, the cabin air let out through the hatch, and the cabin's breathing until the next walk.
cons: Low pressure: 41 % cannot fill a suit
parts.real: 50-litre steel oxygen cylinder at 150 bar

parts.name: High-pressure oxygen tank
parts.desc: 36 kg of oxygen at 414 bar, like the ISS's NORS tanks.
parts.role: Two EVA refills in one tank.
parts.detail: A NORS-class composite tank at 6000 psi: 36 kg of oxygen, 31 kg usable for the suit; about twelve trips outside. One valve for all of it.
pros: Five times the usable oxygen of a bottle
cons: One valve for all of it
parts.real: NORS recharge tank (ISS)

parts.name: CO₂ scrubber
parts.desc: Keeps the cabin air breathable for months.
parts.role: Removes the CO₂ the crew breathes out.
parts.detail: Without a scrubber the cabin fills with carbon dioxide in days. This one works like Orion's: two amine beds take turns, one cleaning the air while space's vacuum empties the other. Apollo 13 used throwaway lithium hydroxide canisters instead.
cons: Can fail: keep LiOH as a backup
parts.real: Orion's amine swing bed (CAMRAS)

parts.name: Radiation shelter
parts.desc: Water-walled corner to hide in during a solar storm.
parts.role: A water-walled corner to hide in during a solar storm.
parts.detail: Between the planets there is no magnetic field to hide behind. When the Sun throws a storm, the crew climbs into this shelter, whose walls are tanks of water, until it passes.
parts.real: Orion storm-shelter concept

parts.name: Water recycler
parts.desc: Recovers about 98 % of the water, like the ISS.
parts.role: Recovers about 98 % of the water.
parts.detail: Turns yesterday's water back into today's. The ISS recovers about 98 %; without it a long trip would need tonnes of water.
parts.real: ISS Water Recovery System

parts.name: Radiator panel
parts.desc: Dumps cabin heat into space; vacuum is a thermos.
parts.role: Dumps cabin heat into space.
parts.detail: Vacuum is a thermos: nothing conducts heat away. A radiator panel sheds the heat from electronics and people by glowing it off into space.
parts.real: Shuttle payload-bay door radiators

parts.name: Escape tower, Mercury type
parts.desc: A solid rocket on a red truss: in an emergency it yanks the capsule off the booster.
parts.role: Pulls the capsule clear of a failing booster in the first minutes of flight.
parts.detail: A three-legged steel truss holds a solid rocket above the capsule. If the booster fails, the motor fires for about a second through three nozzles tilted outward so the flame misses the cabin, and drags the capsule clear; then the capsule's parachutes take over. On a good flight a small jettison motor throws the tower away a couple of minutes up. The real system weighed 460 kg with its ballast; the game's is 350 kg, and since the game drops nothing, it rides to Mars.
pros: Saves the crew in a pad or early-flight explosion
Up to +2 % ship reliability (the whole-ship bonus is capped at 6 %)
Its spike smooths the air over a blunt capsule
cons: Only one escape system counts: a tower and abort pods share one bonus
parts.real: Mercury escape system: Grand Central 1-KS-52000 motor, 52,000 lbf (231 kN) for about 1 s through three canted nozzles; 1,015 lb (460 kg) including 236 lb of ballast

parts.name: Escape tower, Apollo type
parts.desc: A titanium truss with a 650 kN solid motor, canards and a Q-ball nose.
parts.role: Pulls a big command module clear of a failing booster, from the pad to high altitude.
parts.detail: Four titanium legs carry the launch escape motor: four nozzles tilted outward give about 650 kN for three seconds, enough to lift a five-tonne cabin a mile clear. Above it sit the tower jettison motor, a small pitch motor that steers the stack away from the booster, two canards that flip the capsule heat-shield first, and the Q-ball, a nose probe that senses the angle of the airflow. Never needed on an Apollo flight, but carried on every one. The real system weighed about 3.6 t; the game's is scaled down to 4.4 m and 1 t, and since the game drops nothing, it rides to Mars.
pros: Saves the crew from the pad to high altitude
Up to +3 % ship reliability (the whole-ship bonus is capped at 6 %)
cons: Its legs press hard on the nose below it
Only one escape system counts: a tower and abort pods share one bonus
parts.real: Apollo LES: 33 ft (10 m) long, about 8,000 lb (3.6 t); escape motor about 147,000 lbf (654 kN) for 3.2 s; tower jettison motor 31,500 lbf; pitch control motor 2,420 lbf; 10 ft titanium truss

parts.name: Escape tower & fairing, Soyuz type
parts.desc: Tower, fairing and folding grid fins in one escape unit: the system that saved Soyuz T-10a.
parts.role: A fairing over the top of the ship with the escape tower on its nose: in an abort the whole front end flies away with the crew.
parts.detail: On Soyuz the escape tower is bolted to the fairing, not to the capsule. In an abort the motor pulls the fairing and the modules inside it off the rocket, four grid fins fold out to keep it flying straight, and the capsule drops out on its parachute. In 1983 it fired seconds before Soyuz T-10a exploded on the pad: the crew pulled 14 to 17 g and walked away. Small motors on the fairing itself cover the minutes after the tower is gone; they saved Soyuz MS-10 in 2018. The real escape module weighs 7.6 t, but that counts the two crew modules it pulls away; the game's tower and fairing are 1.4 t, and they ride to Mars.
pros: The only escape system that has saved a crew from a pad explosion
Up to +3 % ship reliability (the whole-ship bonus is capped at 6 %)
cons: Big side area high up: pulls the centre of pressure forward
Only one escape system counts: a tower and abort pods share one bonus
parts.real: Soyuz SAS: escape module 7,635 kg, up to 76 t (745 kN) of thrust from about 4 t of solid propellant, four folding stabilisers; Soyuz T-10a (1983), MS-10 (2018)

parts.name: Launch abort system, Orion type
parts.desc: A solid tower with reverse-flow nozzles and its own steering motor: the strongest escape system built.
parts.role: Pulls the crew module away and steers it, from the pad to the edge of space.
parts.detail: No truss: the abort motor stands on a cap over the crew module's nose. Its gas flows up the motor and turns back out through four nozzles near its top, so the tower can be short and the flame starts far from the capsule. Above it are the jettison motor, which pulls the tower away on a normal flight, and at the very top, under the nose cone, the attitude control motor: a ring of eight valves on a solid gas generator that steers the whole stack. Tested on the pad in 2010 and at the worst air load in 2019. The real system weighs about 7 t; the game's is scaled to 1.25 t, and it rides to Mars.
pros: Strongest push of any escape system
Up to +3.5 % ship reliability (the whole-ship bonus is capped at 6 %)
cons: Only one escape system counts: a tower and abort pods share one bonus
parts.real: Orion LAS: abort motor about 400,000 lbf (1.8 MN), attitude control motor up to 7,000 lbf of steering force, jettison motor over 40,000 lbf; Pad Abort-1 (2010), Ascent Abort-2 (2019)

parts.name: Boost protective cover
parts.desc: Fibreglass and cork over the capsule's nose; the escape tower stands on it.
parts.role: Keeps the heat of the climb and the escape motor's flame off the capsule's nose and windows, and carries the tower.
parts.detail: On Apollo a fibreglass shell covered with cork wrapped the whole command module during the climb, so air friction and the exhaust of the escape motor could not scorch the windows and the hatch, and it left with the tower. The game draws only its top: the collar between the capsule's docking tunnel and the tower's legs, 150 kg instead of the real 318 kg.
pros: A solid base for a tower
cons: Mass that does nothing after the climb
parts.real: Apollo boost protective cover: about 700 lb (318 kg) of fibreglass, honeycomb and cork over the whole command module

parts.name: Hinged nose cap
parts.desc: A dome over the docking port that swings open in orbit.
parts.role: Smooths the capsule's nose on the way up and keeps the docking port clean; opens on a hinge in space.
parts.detail: A capsule's nose holds the docking port and its soft-capture ring, which would catch the air on the climb and the heat on the way home. Crew Dragon covers it with a dome that swings aside on a hinge once in orbit and closes again before re-entry. Less drag than a bare nose.
pros: Less drag than a bare capsule nose
cons: A hinge that must close before re-entry
parts.real: Crew Dragon hinged nosecone (Cargo Dragon 1 threw its nose cone away after launch)

parts.name: Recovery nose section
parts.desc: The capsule's own nose: main parachute, re-entry thrusters and a rendezvous radar.
parts.role: A narrow nose on the capsule that packs the main parachute, the re-entry thrusters and a radar for finding other spacecraft.
parts.detail: Gemini had no fairing and no tower: its nose was this section. Inside, the drogue and an 84-ft ringsail main parachute; below them, the thrusters that held the capsule steady through re-entry; on the tip, the radar that found the Agena target for the first dockings. Gemini crews would have escaped on ejection seats instead (an option inside the cabin).
cons: Blunt: more drag than a fairing
parts.real: Gemini rendezvous and recovery section: 84-ft (25.6 m) ringsail main parachute, drogue and pilot chutes, rendezvous radar

parts.name: Von Kármán nose
parts.desc: The least-drag curve for its length and width: less drag than any other nose of its size.
parts.role: A nose shaped by the mathematics of least drag.
parts.detail: Theodore von Kármán worked out the nose curve with the least drag for a given length and base: a slightly rounder tip and a slimmer shoulder than an ogive. The curve bends two ways at once, so its panels are harder to lay up and the price goes up.
pros: Least drag of any medium nose
cons: Compound curves: more expensive to make
parts.real: Haack series with C = 0 (LD-Haack, the von Kármán ogive): the minimum-drag nose for a given length and diameter

parts.name: Biconic nose
parts.desc: Two straight cones: cheap to build from flat panels.
parts.role: A cone on a cone: simple to make, a little more drag than a curved nose.
parts.detail: A biconic nose is two straight cones: a slender one at the base and a blunter one at the tip. Every panel can be rolled from a flat sheet, so it is cheap and quick to make, and the blunt tip stands the heat of a fast climb. The kink between the cones adds a little drag.
parts.real: Delta II 9.5-ft (2.9 m) aluminium fairing: hemispherical cap, a biconic nose of 20° and 15°, 8.49 m long; also cone-on-cone noses on many sounding rockets

parts.name: Composite fairing, 5 m class
parts.desc: Two carbon-fibre halves around a big payload, thrown off once the air is thin.
parts.role: A large two-piece fairing of carbon fibre on aluminium honeycomb, with a boat-tail down to the capsule.
parts.detail: Big modern fairings are two halves of carbon-fibre skin over an aluminium honeycomb core, joined along a separation rail. Gas pushers or a pyrotechnic cord split them and they fall away. A boat-tail at the bottom narrows to whatever sits under it. Its skin takes one debris strike for what is inside.
pros: Shields the top from one hit
cons: Big side area high on the ship
parts.real: Falcon 9 fairing: 5.2 m × 13.2 m, carbon fibre on a 25 mm aluminium honeycomb core, helium pneumatic pushers; halves recovered and reflown

parts.name: Ablative heat shield, small
parts.desc: A small ablative dish for a one-seat capsule.
parts.role: An ablative shield sized for the small capsule.
parts.detail: Mercury's shield was fibreglass soaked in resin, built up in layers to char away slowly. Small and light, but a small shield means a small drag area: in thin Martian air the ship falls faster and the engines must do more of the braking.
cons: Entry drag area 45 m² against 80 for the medium shield: the engines must brake harder at Mars
parts.real: Mercury orbital heat shield: 1.89 m across, fibreglass and phenolic resin ablator

parts.name: Unpressurised trunk
parts.desc: A hollow section under the heat shield with solar cells and radiators on its skin.
parts.role: The section under the capsule that carries solar cells, radiators and cargo, and joins the capsule to the stage.
parts.detail: Crew Dragon rides on a trunk: an unpressurised cylinder with solar cells on one side of its skin, radiators on the other, and small fins that keep the capsule flying nose-first during an abort. Starliner and Orion use a service module in the same place. Here it adds power and a place to clamp more equipment.
cons: Side area high on the ship
parts.real: Crew Dragon trunk: body-mounted solar cells, radiators and abort fins; thrown away before re-entry

parts.name: Main parachute cluster
parts.desc: Three big ringsail mains in one pack: the ship lands safely on two.
parts.role: Three main parachutes that open together; one can fail and the other two still land the ship.
parts.detail: Crewed capsules hang under a cluster, not a single canopy. Apollo flew three 25.5 m ringsails, and Apollo 15 came down safely on two when one collapsed. Orion flies three. The packs sit side by side and are pulled out together by pilot chutes once the drogues have slowed the capsule.
pros: Twice the drag of one supersonic chute
cons: Opens lower and slower than the supersonic chute
parts.real: Apollo: 3 × 83.5 ft (25.5 m) ringsails; Orion: 3 × 116 ft (35 m) ringsails

parts.name: Abort engine pod
parts.desc: Two hypergolic engines in the capsule wall that push it away from a failing rocket.
parts.role: A pusher escape system: engines built into the capsule instead of a tower on top.
parts.detail: Instead of a tower that pulls, Crew Dragon pushes: eight SuperDraco engines in four pods around its wall, 71 kN each, light within a fraction of a second and shove the capsule clear. Nothing is thrown away on a good flight, and the propellant also feeds the steering thrusters. A set is four pods, one on each side; the reliability bonus counts once for the whole escape system, so pods and a tower together are no safer than the better of the two.
pros: Works from the pad to orbit
Up to +2.5 % ship reliability for the whole set (the whole-ship bonus is capped at 6 %)
cons: 130 kg each, and a set is four
Only one escape system counts: a tower and abort pods share one bonus
parts.real: SuperDraco: 71 kN (16,000 lbf), 3D-printed Inconel chamber, 8 per Crew Dragon in 4 pods; Starliner: 4 RS-88 abort engines at 40,000 lbf (180 kN) each

parts.name: LiOH canisters
parts.desc: Throw-away cartridges that soak up CO₂: simple, cheap, and they run out.
parts.role: Lithium hydroxide cartridges that absorb the carbon dioxide the crew breathes out.
parts.detail: Cabin air is blown through lithium hydroxide, which binds the carbon dioxide; when a cartridge is full it is swapped for a fresh one, about every twelve hours. No power, nothing to break, but they are used up. Apollo 13's crew had to tape the command module's square canisters into the lunar module's round sockets.
cons: Used up: enough for weeks, not months
parts.real: Apollo command module LiOH canisters (square; the lunar module's were round); still a backup on the ISS

parts.name: Vostok sphere
parts.desc: A metal sphere for one, coated all over in ablator: it needs no separate heat shield and comes home whichever way it falls.
parts.role: The cabin and its own heat shield in one: a ball that is safe at any angle.
parts.detail: Vostok's cabin was a sphere 2.3 m across with ablator over its whole skin, so it needed no steering on the way down: a ball has no wrong way round. Its centre of mass sat low, so it turned itself to fall the same way every time. The price is a steep, unguided fall of about 8 to 9 g, and a capsule that cannot glide toward a landing spot. On Vostok the cosmonaut ejected at about 7 km and landed on his own parachute.
pros: Heat shield built in: no separate shield part
cons: Entry drag area 45 against 80 for a medium shield
parts.real: Vostok 3KA descent module: sphere 2.3 m across, about 2,400–2,460 kg, ablator over the whole sphere (1961–63)

parts.name: Mercury capsule
parts.desc: America's first: a one-seat cone of dark metal shingles with a narrow neck for the parachutes and a canister of antennas on top.
parts.role: A one-seat cabin under an escape tower: the smallest crew capsule America built.
parts.detail: A titanium pressure shell inside a cone of René 41 nickel-alloy shingles, with a beryllium-covered neck above it that holds the drogue and the 63-ft ringsail main. The astronaut lay on a couch moulded to his body. On the way home the heat shield dropped 1.2 m on a rubberised skirt that filled with air to soften the splash.
pros: Flown six times with a crew
cons: Small: only 200 W of its own power
parts.real: Mercury spacecraft 1959–63: 1.89 m across the heat shield and about 2.9 m from the shield to the top of the antenna canister; 1,360–1,830 kg; René 41 shingles; 7.9 m tall with the escape tower

parts.name: Gemini capsule
parts.desc: Two seats side by side, each under its own hatch, in a black cone of shingles. The crew escaped on ejection seats, not a tower.
parts.role: A two-seat cabin that could steer itself on the way home.
parts.detail: An enlarged Mercury: two seats under two hatches that opened for spacewalks, beaded René 41 shingles outside, and below the nose a ring of sixteen thrusters in two independent sets. The capsule was flown slightly off-centre so it generated lift and could be steered toward the recovery ships. Its nose section carried the parachutes and a radar, and its white adapter below carried fuel cells and manoeuvring thrusters.
cons: Cramped: the size of a car's front seat
No escape tower: ejection seats only
parts.real: Gemini re-entry module 1964–66: 2.29 m at the base, 3.45 m long (cabin 1.79 m, RCS section 0.46 m, nose section 1.2 m), 1,983 kg; beaded René 41 shingles; two ejection seats

parts.name: Apollo command module
parts.desc: The cone that went to the Moon: three couches, five windows and a skin of silver film over the heat shield.
parts.role: A three-seat cabin built to come home from the Moon at 11 km/s.
parts.detail: An aluminium honeycomb pressure shell inside a steel honeycomb heat-shield structure, covered in Avcoat and wrapped in silver Mylar. The sidewall slopes at about 32.5°, so the capsule flies tilted and makes lift, which let the crew steer the entry. At the top, under a forward heat shield, sit the docking tunnel, the drogues and the three ringsail mains. Its oxygen and power came from the service module below.
pros: Built for the fastest crewed return ever flown
cons: Power and oxygen live in the service module
parts.real: Apollo CM 1966–75: 3.91 m wide, 3.48 m tall with the probe, 5,560 kg; Avcoat 5026-39G in about 360,000 honeycomb cells; backshell about 32.5° (33° often quoted)

parts.name: Soyuz descent module
parts.desc: The "headlight": a rounded bell for three, the most-flown crew capsule there is. It lands on the steppe with a last-second rocket kick.
parts.role: A three-seat capsule shaped like a car headlight, built to land on solid ground.
parts.detail: A small bell: a spherical heat shield at the base, a gentle 7° cone and a round top with the hatch into the orbital module. Its centre of mass is off the axis, so it flies at an angle and makes a little lift. The crew lie in seats with liners moulded to each body. Below 6 km the heat shield drops off, and about a metre above the ground six small solid rockets fire to cut the speed to a couple of metres per second.
cons: Everything else lives in the other two modules
parts.real: Soyuz TMA/MS descent module: 2.17 m × 2.24 m, about 2,950 kg; glass-phenolic ablator; six soft-landing engines (since 1967)

parts.name: Shenzhou re-entry module
parts.desc: China's crew capsule: a Soyuz-shaped bell grown 15 % wider, for three.
parts.role: A three-seat headlight-shaped capsule that lands on land.
parts.detail: Shenzhou follows the Soyuz layout, built bigger and new: a re-entry module 2.52 m across between an orbital module and a service module. It falls under one 1,200 m² ringsail with a 760 m² spare, drops its heat shield low down and fires four small solid rockets a metre above the ground.
parts.real: Shenzhou re-entry module (since 1999): 2.52 m wide, 3,240 kg, heat shield 450 kg; main chute 1,200 m², backup 760 m²

parts.name: Orion crew module
parts.desc: Apollo's shape, half again as wide: four seats, silver tiles on the backshell and an Avcoat shield of 186 blocks.
parts.role: A four-seat deep-space capsule, the widest crew capsule flown.
parts.detail: Orion keeps Apollo's blunt cone and its lifting entry, scaled up to 5 m. The backshell is covered in about 1,300 silica tiles under a silver coating, the heat shield in Avcoat blocks. At the top, under a forward bay cover, are the docking system and the parachutes: three small chutes to pull the cover off, two drogues, three pilots and three 35 m mains. It came home from the Moon on Artemis I in 2022.
parts.real: Orion CM: 5.03 m × 3.35 m, about 9.3 t at liftoff (Artemis I); 186 Avcoat blocks, about 1,300 AETB-8 backshell tiles; 11 parachutes

parts.name: Dragon capsule
parts.desc: A tall, steep capsule with a black PICA-3 heat shield under it and room for four, flown again and again.
parts.role: A four-seat capsule with a steep wall, its own abort engines and a hinged nose cone.
parts.detail: Dragon has a steeper, taller wall than Apollo or Orion, so the same width holds more room. Sixteen Draco thrusters steer it, and the eight SuperDraco abort engines sit in four bulges low on the wall. A PICA-3 heat shield is under the base (Dragon 1 flew PICA-X); the hinged nose cone protects the docking port. Capsules are refurbished and flown several times.
cons: Tall wall: more side area high on the ship
parts.real: Crew Dragon (since 2019): 4 m wide, capsule 4.5 m tall with its nose cone, 8.1 m with the trunk; 16 Draco thrusters (400 N), 8 SuperDracos (71 kN); PICA-3 heat shield

parts.name: Starliner crew module
parts.desc: Boeing's blunt cone for up to seven, with a weldless shell, a forward heat shield over its parachutes and airbags for a landing on the ground.
parts.role: A reusable crew capsule that lands in the desert on airbags.
parts.detail: Starliner's pressure shell is spun and machined with no welds. On the way home the forward heat shield pops off to free the drogues and three mains, then the base heat shield drops and six airbags inflate under the capsule for a landing in New Mexico. Its two crewed-era test flights found software faults (2019) and thruster trouble in its service module (2024), when the crew came home on another ship.
parts.real: Starliner (since 2019): CM + SM 5 m tall and 4.6 m wide; Boeing Lightweight Ablator; 2 drogues, 3 mains, 6 airbags; CFT 5 Jun 2024, capsule landed uncrewed 7 Sep 2024

parts.name: Gaganyaan crew module
parts.desc: India's capsule for three: a double-walled cone that splashes down in the Bay of Bengal under three mains.
parts.role: A three-seat capsule with a metal pressure shell inside an outer shell that carries the heat protection.
parts.detail: The Gaganyaan crew module has two walls: an inner metal cabin that holds the air and an outer shell for the heat protection. It comes home under ten parachutes in sequence (two apex-cover chutes, two drogues, three pilots, three mains). A test module flew an abort in October 2023 (TV-D1) and splashed down at 8.5 m/s.
parts.real: Gaganyaan crew module (ISRO): a pressurised metal cabin inside an outer shell; the TV-D1 test module was 3.1 m wide, 2.97 m tall and 4,520 kg (21 Oct 2023)

parts.name: New Shepard capsule
parts.desc: A six-seat tourist capsule with the biggest windows flown and an escape motor built into its base. Made for a ten-minute hop: it has no shield for orbital speed.
parts.role: A suborbital capsule: six seats, huge windows and its own escape motor underneath.
parts.detail: New Shepard's capsule rides on top of its booster with no fairing. A solid escape motor in its base pushes it away from a failing booster; it did so for real on the uncrewed NS-23 flight in 2022, and the capsule landed safely. It comes down under three mains (it can land on one), and a retro-thrust system and a crushable ring take the last of the speed. It never flies at orbital speed, so it carries no shield for an entry from orbit.
pros: Escape motor built in: up to +2 % ship reliability (counts once with any other escape system)
parts.real: New Shepard crew capsule (since 2015, crewed since 2021): 6 seats, 15 m³, 6 large windows, 3 mains; a solid escape motor under the floor, used on NS-23 (12 Sep 2022)

parts.name: Mengzhou crew module
parts.desc: China's new reusable cone for up to seven, with its heat shield built in. Its prototype flew in 2020 and landed on airbags.
parts.role: A large reusable crew capsule for low orbit and the Moon.
parts.detail: Mengzhou breaks from the Soyuz-style Shenzhou: a big Apollo-like cone, a reusable crew module and a throw-away service module. A full-size prototype flew to orbit on a Long March 5B in May 2020, came back above 9 km/s and landed on airbags under three parachutes; pad and Max-Q abort tests followed in 2025 and 2026.
parts.real: Mengzhou: a reusable crew module and an expendable service module; full-size prototype on Long March 5B, 5 May 2020 (above 9 km/s on the way back, airbag landing); pad abort 17 Jun 2025; Max-Q abort 11 Feb 2026

parts.name: Dream Chaser spaceplane
parts.desc: A small winged lifting body that glides home to a runway. It rides nose-up inside a fairing with its wings folded.
parts.role: A lifting body: a cabin with its heat protection built into its belly, landing on a runway.
parts.detail: Dream Chaser descends from NASA's HL-20 design: a flat-bottomed body that makes lift by its shape, with small wings that fold to fit a 5 m fairing. Silica tiles and a toughened nose cap protect its belly, so it lands like a glider on a runway. The cargo version was built for station supply; a crewed version for seven was proposed to NASA. It has not flown in space yet (first free-flight demonstration targeted for late 2026).
pros: Heat protection built in: no separate shield part
Glides to a runway: a gentle landing
cons: Entry drag area 60: a glider falls fast through thin air
parts.real: Sierra Space Dream Chaser (Tenacity): about 9 m long, wings that fold for the 5.4 m fairing of Vulcan, silica tiles and a toughened nose cap; first flight a free-flying demonstration

parts.name: Starship nose
parts.desc: A stainless-steel ogive with black tiles on its belly side and two flaps: the nose of the ship built to land on Mars.
parts.role: The forward section of a steel ship that falls belly-first and flips upright to land on its engines.
parts.detail: Starship has no capsule: the whole ship comes home. Its nose is the same stainless steel as its tanks, with hexagonal ceramic tiles pinned to the side that faces the air, and two forward flaps that steer the belly-first fall. The crew area would sit inside this nose; none has flown yet. Test flights since 2023 have lost tiles and several ships.
pros: Steel is cheap and takes heat
The whole side of the ship brakes: entry drag area 150
Pointed nose: low drag on the way up
cons: Tiles can crack or fall off on the climb
No crew has flown in it
parts.real: SpaceX Starship upper stage: 9 m wide, about 50 m tall, stainless steel, hexagonal heat-shield tiles and two forward flaps; test flights since 2023; no crew cabin has flown

parts.name: Backup retro-rocket
parts.desc: A small solid motor bolted on top of the capsule: a second way to slow down for the trip home.
parts.role: A spare braking motor in case the main retro engine fails.
parts.detail: Vostok had one retro engine and no backup: if it failed, the cosmonaut would wait about ten days for the orbit to decay. Voskhod flew higher, so a 145 kg solid motor sat on top of the sphere as a spare. Reliability +0.5 %.
cons: 160 kg that is usually never fired
parts.real: Voskhod backup solid retro-rocket, 145 kg, on the nose of the descent module (1964–65)

parts.name: Soyuz orbital module
parts.desc: A round living room on the capsule's nose: the toilet, the stores, a docking port at the front, and an airlock for spacewalks.
parts.role: Living space and the docking port, thrown away before the trip home.
parts.detail: The orbital module is why three people fit in Soyuz: the capsule is only for launch and landing, and this nearly spherical room above it holds the toilet, food, a window for docking, and the SSVP docking probe at the front. It has three hatches and can serve as an airlock. It is cut loose before entry, so its mass never has to be protected from the heat.
parts.real: Soyuz TMA/MS orbital module: 2.26 m × 2.98 m, about 1,350 kg; SSVP docking unit; three hatches

parts.name: Shenzhou orbital module
parts.desc: A cylinder with its own solar wings, left behind in orbit to keep working as a small satellite.
parts.role: Living space, the docking port and an airlock, with its own power.
parts.detail: Unlike the Soyuz orbital module, Shenzhou's has its own solar panels and thrusters: after the crew leave it, it keeps flying for months as an experiment platform. From Shenzhou 8 it carries an androgynous docking ring based on APAS.
parts.real: Shenzhou orbital module: 2.25 m × 2.80 m, 1,500 kg, own solar arrays; APAS-derived docking from Shenzhou 8 (2011)

parts.name: Progress cargo module
parts.desc: Soyuz's orbital module turned into a pantry: food, water, air bottles and spare parts, with the docking probe on its nose.
parts.role: A pressurised cargo hold with a docking probe; includes one spare oxygen supply.
parts.detail: Progress is Soyuz with the crew taken out: the orbital module becomes a 7 m³ cargo hold, the descent module is replaced by tanks of propellant and water, and the service module stays the same. It docks automatically with the Kurs radar. Here its hold carries one spare oxygen supply.
parts.real: Progress MS (since 2015): 7.4 m × 2.7 m, about 7,300–7,440 kg; cargo module, refuelling module, service module; up to 2,600 kg cargo

parts.name: Cygnus pressurised module
parts.desc: The cargo cylinder of Northrop Grumman's Cygnus: packed with supplies, it is a pantry and a storm shelter in one.
parts.role: A pressurised hold full of food, water and air; its packed walls double as a radiation shelter.
parts.detail: Cygnus's pressurised module comes from Thales Alenia's station modules and is berthed by the station's robot arm to a wide square hatch. NASA's Gateway habitat HALO is built from the same design. Packed with water and food, a hold like this is a good place to wait out a solar storm, which is how the game counts it, with one spare oxygen supply.
cons: Berths with a robot arm, cannot dock itself
parts.real: Cygnus Enhanced (since 2015): 3.07 m wide, 6.39 m long with its service module, 3,500 kg cargo; XL 8.0 m (2024); flew in the Atlas V 4 m fairing and on Falcon 9

parts.name: HTV logistics carrier
parts.desc: Japan's Kounotori: a pressurised hold with a big square hatch, and an open bay below it for outside cargo.
parts.role: The biggest hold of any supply ship: a storm shelter and a spare oxygen supply in the game.
parts.detail: HTV's pressurised carrier has a 1.2 m square hatch so whole refrigerator-sized racks fit through, and below it an unpressurised bay with an exposed pallet for batteries and experiments. All nine HTVs reached the station (2009–2020). Here, packed with water and food, it serves as the storm shelter.
parts.real: HTV (Kounotori) 2009–20: about 10 m long, 4.4 m wide, about 16.5 t; about 6 t cargo; berthed by the station arm; HTV-X since 2025

parts.name: ATV cargo carrier
parts.desc: Europe's supply ship: a pressurised hold with a Russian docking probe on its nose, and tanks of water, air and propellant round it.
parts.role: A hold that docks by itself and carries water, air and fuel as well as dry cargo.
parts.detail: ATV's integrated cargo carrier docked automatically to the back of the station's Russian segment and also pushed the station to a higher orbit. Five flew (2008–2014); their propulsion section became the European Service Module of Orion. Here it carries a spare oxygen supply and counts as a storm shelter.
parts.real: ATV (2008–14): 10.3 m long, 4.5 m wide, 20,750 kg; Russian probe docking; 855 kg water, 102 kg gas among 6.6 t of cargo

parts.name: Vostok instrument module
parts.desc: Two cones joined at their bases, ringed with gas bottles, with the retro engine underneath.
parts.role: Batteries, gas, cooling louvres and the one retro engine that brings Vostok home.
parts.detail: Below the sphere hangs a double cone carrying the batteries, the radio, cooling shutters, a ring of spherical bottles of nitrogen and oxygen for the attitude jets and the cabin, and the TDU retro engine: 16 kN for about 42 seconds. It separates before entry and burns up.
cons: Batteries only: 250 W for about ten days
parts.real: Vostok instrument module: double cone about 2.4 m across, 2,300 kg; TDU retro engine about 16 kN, Isp 266 s; cold nitrogen attitude jets in two systems of 10 kg of gas

parts.name: Mercury retropack
parts.desc: Three small solid rockets strapped to the middle of the heat shield: fired one after another, they start the fall home.
parts.role: The braking rockets for the trip home, held on the heat shield by three straps.
parts.detail: Mercury had no service module. Its retro package sat on the heat shield: three solid retro-rockets of 4.45 kN for about 10 s, fired five seconds apart so a failure of one would not tip the capsule, and three small posigrade rockets that pushed the capsule off the rocket. After retrofire the straps were cut and the pack fell away. On Friendship 7 it was kept on through entry because a sensor warned the shield might be loose.
cons: Mass that does no work on the way up
parts.real: Mercury retropackage: three TE-M-316 solid retro-rockets of 4.45 kN for about 10 s, and three posigrade rockets of 1.78 kN for 1 s

parts.name: Gemini adapter module
parts.desc: A white flared skirt behind the capsule: fuel cells, oxygen, manoeuvring thrusters and four retro-rockets.
parts.role: Power, oxygen and the thrusters that let Gemini change its orbit.
parts.detail: Gemini's adapter was a white magnesium cone flaring from the 2.29 m capsule to the 3.05 m rocket. The equipment section held the first fuel cells ever flown, the oxygen, and the sixteen OAMS thrusters that let Gemini change orbit and rendezvous; the retrograde section held four solid retros. Its white skin was the radiator. A stuck OAMS thruster set Gemini 8 spinning in 1966.
parts.real: Gemini adapter: magnesium, white ceramic paint; 3.05 m (120 in) at the base, 2.24 m (88.3 in) at the top, 2.29 m long (equipment section 1.4 m, retro section 0.89 m); fuel cells (Gemini 5 on), OAMS 16 thrusters, 4 TE-M-385 retros (11 kN for 5.5 s each)

parts.name: Apollo service module
parts.desc: The silver cylinder behind the command module: fuel cells, cryogenic oxygen, four thruster quads and the big engine bell.
parts.role: Power, oxygen and the engine for the trip home, thrown away just before entry.
parts.detail: Six wedge-shaped bays round a central tunnel held the SPS engine's propellant, three fuel cells, and the cryogenic oxygen and hydrogen tanks; radiator panels and four quads of R-4D thrusters sat on the skin. Its engine (91 kN) put Apollo into lunar orbit and brought it home. An oxygen tank in bay 4 exploded on Apollo 13 in 1970, and the crew came home in the lunar module. In the game the ship's main engines do the pushing; its engine counts as the backup.
cons: Tall: a long cylinder high on the ship
parts.real: Apollo SM: 3.9 m wide, 24 ft 2 in (7.37 m) high including the engine bell, 11,500 lb (5.2 t) dry and 55,000 lb (25 t) loaded; SPS engine 20,500 lbf (91 kN); three fuel cells; four quads of 100 lbf thrusters. The game part keeps the cylinder and the top of the bell, whose lower part sat inside the lunar-module adapter

parts.name: Soyuz service module
parts.desc: The green-blanketed drum at the back of Soyuz: engine, tanks, thrusters and the two solar wings.
parts.role: Propulsion, power and cooling for Soyuz.
parts.detail: An instrument compartment and a propulsion compartment in one drum, under green insulation blankets: the main engine (2.95 kN), 28 small thrusters, the tanks, the radiator and two solar wings spanning 10.7 m. It separates just before entry and burns up.
parts.real: Soyuz TMA/MS service module: 2.72 m × 2.26 m, 2,900 kg; KTDU-80 main engine 2.95 kN, 28 DPO-B thrusters (MS); span 10.7 m

parts.name: Soyuz 7K-OK service module
parts.desc: The first Soyuz's service module, with angled solar wings and a ring-shaped tank round its engines.
parts.role: Propulsion, power and cooling for the first-generation Soyuz.
parts.detail: The 7K-OK flew with its solar panels angled back and an external toroidal tank round the engine section, both dropped in later versions. Its first crewed flight, Soyuz 1 in 1967, ended in a crash when the main parachute did not come out.
parts.real: Soyuz 7K-OK (1966–70): body 2.2 m, at most 2.72 m wide, with angled solar panels and an external ring-shaped tank round the engine section

parts.name: Shenzhou service module
parts.desc: A drum with four main engines and two big rectangular solar wings.
parts.role: Propulsion, power and cooling for Shenzhou.
parts.detail: Four 2.5 kN main engines on nitrogen tetroxide and monomethylhydrazine, small thrusters, the radiators and two large solar wings, the biggest on any capsule of its time.
parts.real: Shenzhou service module: about 2.5 m (2.8 m with its skirt), 2.94 m long, 3,000 kg; 4 × 2.5 kN main engines; span 17 m

parts.name: European Service Module
parts.desc: Orion's service module, built in Europe from the ATV supply ship: four solar wings, 33 engines, and the crew's oxygen and water.
parts.role: Power, propulsion, air and water for Orion; under three white panels at launch.
parts.detail: ESA's service module carries the propellant, oxygen, nitrogen and water, four solar wings spanning 19 m, and 33 engines: one main engine (a refurbished Space Shuttle OMS engine), eight auxiliary engines that can stand in for it, and 24 small thrusters. Three panels cover it during launch and fall away afterwards.
cons: Under three panels: no wings until they open
parts.real: Orion ESM (Airbus for ESA): a little over 5 m across with its structure, 4 m tall, 13.5 t; main engine 6,000 lbf, 8 × 110 lbf, 24 × 50 lbf; arrays 19 m span

parts.name: Dragon 1 trunk
parts.desc: The first Dragon's short trunk, with two solar wings that unfold from its sides.
parts.role: Power and room for outside cargo for the first Dragon.
parts.detail: Cargo Dragon 1 (2010–2020) carried two deployable solar arrays on its trunk, folded under covers for launch, and room inside for unpressurised cargo.
parts.real: Dragon 1 trunk: 2.3 m long (standard) or 4.3 m (extended), with two solar arrays of 4 kW peak (2010–20)

parts.name: Starliner service module
parts.desc: A short drum with four big abort engines, 48 thrusters and an aeroskirt that smooths the join to the rocket.
parts.role: Propulsion, power and the pusher escape system for Starliner.
parts.detail: Starliner's escape system is in its service module: four RS-88-derived engines of 40,000 lbf each push the capsule away from a failing rocket. Around them, twenty OMAC thrusters and 28 small ones; on the base, solar cells. In 2024 several of its thrusters overheated near the station and the crew came home months later on Crew Dragon.
pros: Pusher escape built in: up to +2.5 % ship reliability (counts once with any other escape system)
parts.real: Starliner service module: four 40,000 lbf launch abort engines, 20 OMAC thrusters (about 1,500 lbf) and 28 × 85 lbf thrusters; over 2,900 W from solar cells

parts.name: Gaganyaan service module
parts.desc: India's service module: five engines, sixteen thrusters and solar wings.
parts.role: Propulsion, power and cooling for Gaganyaan.
parts.detail: Five 440 N engines and sixteen 100 N thrusters on MMH and MON-3, tanks, radiators and solar panels. It separates before entry.
parts.real: Gaganyaan service module: five 440 N engines and sixteen 100 N thrusters on MMH and MON-3, with solar panels

parts.name: Mengzhou service module
parts.desc: The throw-away service module of China's new crew ship.
parts.role: Propulsion and power for Mengzhou.
parts.detail: Mengzhou's service module carries the propellant, the main engines and the power system, and is discarded before entry, while the crew module is flown again.
parts.real: Mengzhou service module: propellant, engines and power; thrown away before entry while the crew module is flown again

parts.name: Cygnus service module
parts.desc: A satellite bus with two round fan-shaped solar arrays that open like paper fans.
parts.role: Power, propulsion and guidance for Cygnus.
parts.detail: Built from Northrop Grumman's satellite buses: avionics, tanks, a main engine and thrusters, and two UltraFlex arrays that unfold into circles.
parts.real: Cygnus service module: GEOStar/LEOStar-derived bus, two UltraFlex circular arrays, about 3.5 kW

parts.name: HTV propulsion module
parts.desc: HTV's avionics and propulsion sections: four main thrusters, 28 small ones and solar cells all over the skin.
parts.role: Guidance, power and propulsion for HTV.
parts.detail: The avionics module guides the ship to a point 10 m below the station, where the arm catches it; the propulsion module carries four main thrusters and 28 attitude thrusters. Solar cells cover the outside of the whole ship.
parts.real: HTV avionics and propulsion modules; solar cells mounted on the body of the whole ship

parts.name: ATV propulsion spacecraft
parts.desc: ATV's engine section, with four solar wings in an X: the ancestor of Orion's service module.
parts.role: Propulsion and power for ATV.
parts.detail: Four main engines, 28 thrusters and four solar wings arranged in an X spanning 22.3 m, about 4.8 kW. Its design became the European Service Module.
parts.real: ATV propulsion spacecraft: four X-shaped arrays 22.3 m span, about 4.8 kW average

parts.name: Shooting Star cargo module
parts.desc: The cargo module behind Dream Chaser: solar arrays, extra cargo room, and a bin for station rubbish that burns up.
parts.role: Power and extra cargo room for Dream Chaser.
parts.detail: Shooting Star rides behind the spaceplane, gives it power from its solar arrays and room for unpressurised cargo, and is let go to burn up before the spaceplane glides home.
parts.real: Shooting Star cargo module: about 4.6 m long, solar arrays of up to 6 kW, six thrusters

parts.name: Mars cruise stage
parts.desc: A flat ring of solar cells and radiators that flew Curiosity and Perseverance to Mars, spinning slowly.
parts.role: Power, steering and cooling for the seven-month cruise to Mars.
parts.detail: The cruise stage is a ring on top of the aeroshell's backshell: solar cells on its face, radiators round its rim, hydrazine thrusters to adjust the course, and a pumped-fluid loop to carry heat away. It spins slowly for stability and is cut loose ten minutes before entry.
cons: Power falls as the ship nears Mars
parts.real: Mars Science Laboratory and Mars 2020 cruise stage: a ring of solar cells and radiators about 4 m across, eight hydrazine thrusters and a pumped heat-rejection loop

parts.name: Vostok shroud
parts.desc: A pointed shroud over the sphere, thrown off two and a half minutes up, with no escape tower.
parts.role: Shields the sphere from the air on the climb.
parts.detail: The R-7 carried Vostok inside a slim shroud that covered the sphere and opened at about 156 seconds, uncovering the cosmonaut's foot window. With no escape tower, the cosmonaut's only way out early in flight was the ejection seat.
parts.real: Vostok-K payload shroud, released about 156 s after launch, uncovering the cosmonaut's foot window (1961–63)

parts.name: Dragon 1 nose cone
parts.desc: A small cone over the first Dragon's berthing hatch, thrown away after launch.
parts.role: Smooths the capsule's nose on the climb and protects the hatch and grapple fixture.
parts.detail: Cargo Dragon 1 was caught by the station's robot arm and berthed to a wide square hatch, so its nose carried no docking ring, just a cone over the hatch that was let go in orbit.
pros: Less drag than a bare nose
cons: Gone after launch: the nose is bare on the way home
parts.real: Dragon 1 nose cone over the berthing hatch and grapple fixture, thrown away after launch (2010–20)

parts.name: New Glenn 7 m fairing
parts.desc: The widest fairing flying: two carbon halves 7 m across.
parts.role: A huge carbon-composite fairing; its skin takes one debris strike for what is inside.
parts.detail: New Glenn's fairing is 7 m wide, about twice the volume of a 5 m fairing, made as two carbon-composite halves. In November 2025 it carried NASA's twin ESCAPADE probes toward Mars.
pros: Shields the top from one hit
cons: Big side area high on the ship
parts.real: New Glenn fairing: 7 m wide, two carbon-composite halves; second flight (13 Nov 2025) launched NASA's ESCAPADE Mars probes

parts.name: H-IIA fairing
parts.desc: Kawasaki's aluminium-honeycomb fairing from Tanegashima, whose halves swing open on hinges.
parts.role: A classic metal-honeycomb fairing with hinged halves.
parts.detail: Japan's H-IIA and H-IIB fairings are aluminium honeycomb panels bolted into two half-shells. An expanding steel tube snaps a row of notched bolts, and each half rotates on a hinge and falls away. The 4 m version launched the UAE's Hope to Mars in 2020; the stretched 5 m version carried every HTV.
parts.real: H-IIA 4S fairing: 4.1 m × 12 m, aluminium honeycomb, notched-bolt separation, halves that swing away on hinges (Kawasaki); launched Hope to Mars in July 2020

parts.name: Long March 5 fairing
parts.desc: China's 5.2 m fairing, which carried Tianwen-1 to Mars and the Mengzhou prototype to orbit.
parts.role: A big composite fairing; its skin takes one debris strike for what is inside.
parts.detail: Long March 5 flies a 5.2 m fairing in a normal and a long version (18.5 m). It launched Tianwen-1, China's first Mars orbiter, lander and rover, in July 2020, and the full-size Mengzhou prototype in May 2020.
pros: Shields the top from one hit
cons: Big side area high on the ship
parts.real: Long March 5 fairing: 5.2 m wide; 12.3 m (normal) and 18.5 m (long, first flown 2020) versions; it launched Tianwen-1 to Mars and the Mengzhou prototype to orbit in 2020

parts.name: PSLV heat shield fairing
parts.desc: India's bulbous metal fairing, wider than the rocket, that launched Mangalyaan to Mars.
parts.role: A riveted aluminium isogrid fairing, bulging out over a narrower rocket.
parts.detail: ISRO calls it the heat shield: a 3.2 m bulb of riveted aluminium isogrid over a 2.8 m rocket, a cone and a spherical cap on top. In November 2013 it carried the Mars Orbiter Mission, which reached Mars on the first try in September 2014.
pros: Room for a payload wider than the rocket
parts.real: PSLV heat shield: 3.2 m × 8.3 m, riveted aluminium isogrid, two halves, over the 2.8 m core (ISRO, HAL brochure)

parts.name: Escape tower & fairing, Shenzhou type
parts.desc: A tall solid-rocket tower on a fairing with four grid fins, as on Long March 2F.
parts.role: Pulls the whole front end of the ship away from a failing rocket, with the crew inside.
parts.detail: Like Soyuz, Shenzhou's escape tower is bolted to the fairing: in an abort, the fairing and the two front modules fly away together, four lattice fins open to steady them, and the capsule drops out under its parachute. The tower leaves about two minutes after launch on a good flight.
pros: Up to +3 % ship reliability (counts once with any other escape system)
parts.real: Shenzhou escape tower and fairing on Long March 2F: 11,260 kg, 15.1 m long, 3.8 m across; tower 8.35 m; jettisoned about T+120 s

parts.name: Crew escape system, Gaganyaan type
parts.desc: India's escape tower on a crew-module fairing with four grid fins, tested in 2023.
parts.role: Pulls the crew module away from a failing rocket, from the pad to high altitude.
parts.detail: Five kinds of solid motor: low-altitude escape motors of 875 kN for an abort near the ground, four high-altitude escape motors of 261 kN for thin air, and motors to pitch and to jettison the tower. Four grid fins on the fairing steady it. On TV-D1 (21 October 2023) it pulled a test module away at Mach 1.2 and 11.7 km.
pros: Up to +3 % ship reliability (counts once with any other escape system)
Separate motors for low and high aborts
parts.real: Gaganyaan crew escape system: 15.5 m long, 4.05 m across, 12.5 t; LEM 875.1 kN; HEM 4 × 260.7 kN; TV-D1 21 Oct 2023 (ISRO)

parts.name: Inflatable airlock
parts.desc: A fabric tube folded against the capsule that inflates into a 2.5 m airlock for a spacewalk.
parts.role: Lets a crew member step outside without emptying the cabin of air.
parts.detail: Voskhod's cabin electronics were cooled by air, so the cabin could not be emptied for a spacewalk. A folded rubberised-fabric tube on the side inflated into an airlock 2.5 m long and 1 m wide inside. Alexei Leonov left it for the first spacewalk on 18 March 1965; his suit ballooned and he had to let air out to get back in. The airlock was thrown away afterwards.
pros: A spacewalk without emptying the cabin
parts.real: Voskhod 2 airlock (18 Mar 1965): 250 kg; stowed 0.70 × 0.77 m, inflated 2.5 m long with 1.0 m inside and 1.2 m outside diameter

parts.name: Single main parachute
parts.desc: One huge canopy and a spare packed beside it, as on Mercury, Vostok, Soyuz and Shenzhou.
parts.role: A main parachute of about 1,000 m² with a smaller reserve.
parts.detail: Soyuz hangs under a single main of about 1,000 m², pulled out by a drogue, with a reserve about half that size in its own container. If the main fails the reserve is fired. On Soyuz 1 in 1967 the main stuck in its container and the reserve tangled with the drogue; Vladimir Komarov was killed. Shenzhou uses a 1,200 m² main.
cons: One canopy carries the whole capsule
parts.real: Soyuz: 24 m² drogue, 1,000 m² main and a reserve about half its size; Shenzhou: 1,200 m² main and 760 m² backup; Mercury: 63 ft ringsail main and a reserve

parts.name: Four-main parachute cluster
parts.desc: Four mains in one pack: the capsule lands safely on three.
parts.role: Four main parachutes that open together, so one can fail.
parts.detail: Crew Dragon flies four mains, pulled out after two drogues have slowed and steadied the capsule. The fourth canopy means one can fail and the splashdown is still within limits. Upgraded Mark 3 chutes have flown since 2019.
pros: The most drag of any chute pack
parts.real: Crew Dragon: two drogues at about 18,000 ft, then four mains at about 6,000 ft (NASA, Demo-2, 2020)

parts.name: H-IIB fairing
parts.desc: The H-IIA's 5 m fairing stretched by 3 m to carry Japan's HTV supply ship.
parts.role: A long aluminium-honeycomb fairing with hinged halves.
parts.detail: For HTV, Kawasaki stretched the 5 m H-IIA fairing by 3 m to 15 m. Like the shorter one, it is aluminium honeycomb in two half-shells that break apart along notched bolts and swing away on hinges.
cons: Long: big side area high on the ship
parts.real: H-IIB 5S-H fairing: 5.1 m × 15 m, the H-IIA 5S stretched by 3 m for HTV (Kawasaki, JAXA, 2009–20)
